newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-BASF nears deal to sell tape unit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BASF nears deal to sell tape unit.

text.p: Germany's BASF AG said on Thursday it will likely complete a deal to sell its tape unit BASF Magnetics GmbH to RAKS Holding in October after its supervisory board agreed to the deal.
"I expect that plans will proceed as discussed and that we can complete due diligence work within four weeks," BASF chief financial officer Max Dietrich Kley told a news conference.

Although the supervisory board agreed to the sale to Turkey's RAKS in principle, it said management should be able to still review any other bids for the ailing tape group, one of the world's best known brands.

BASF, eager to spin off the unit in order to concentrate on its core chemical, drug and agricultural business, prefers to sell the tape business to RAKS since the Turkish group plans to expand this business, giving Magnetics a greater chance of securing jobs.
But Kley said considerable job cuts at BASF Magnetics were unavoidable. He could not detail how many of the current 3,700 jobs at the unit would be lost.
The sale is expected to be completed by January 1997.

BASF has long tried to sell the loss-making Magnetics group. Kley said the parent company could no longer continue propping up the division, which has absorbed 600 million marks ($396.4 million) in subsidies over the last five years.
Reversing an earlier forecast that the division would post a profit this year, Kley said Magnetics was now expected to report a 20 million mark operating loss.

"There comes a time when management cannot continue to support this group," Kley said, vowing the parent company would not infect fresh money into the tape unit, even if Raks were to pull out of the sale negotiations.
"There will be no fresh funds if RAKS pulls out. The Magnetics unit can survive as long as their liquidity allows them to stay afloat."
Kley said that one reason the tape business fared so poorly over the past few years is that prices had fallen much more rapidly than BASF had been able to cut costs.
BASF and RAKS agreed to keep the sale price confidential.
Kley also said BASF was also in the advanced stages of negotiations to sell a 51 percent stake in its fertiliser unit Kali und Salz Beteiligungs AG to Canada's Potash Corporation of Saskatchewan Inc.
Potash had agreed to an option to buy another 25 percent stake in Kali by 1999.
Kley did not reveal a price for the divestment, even though BASF earlier said the price would be below the Kali und Salz share price before the deal was announced.
Although the sale is contingent on cartel authority approval, Kley was confident German officials would approve the deal. --Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525 ($1=1.5134 Mark)
